faq.a: Hypoxic vasoconstriction raises pulmonary artery pressure, forcing the RV to work harder and thicken.
faq.q: Why does chronic lung disease cause RVH?

faq.a: If the underlying pressure overload is removed early, RV wall thickness can regress, but long‑standing fibrosis may be permanent.
A parasternal heave combined with a loud P2 strongly suggests elevated right‑sided pressures.
faq.q: What is the most useful bedside test for RV overload?

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with HIV presents with exertional dyspnoea and peripheral oedema – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform bedside echocardiography to assess RV size and pulmonary pressures, because HIV‑associated pulmonary hypertension is common.
How does RVH differ on ECG from LVH? — RVH shows right‑axis deviation and R>S in V1, whereas LVH shows high voltage QRS in left leads and left‑axis deviation.

A patient with rheumatic mitral stenosis develops RVH – explain the pathophysiology. — Mitral stenosis raises left atrial pressure, leading to pulmonary venous hypertension, then pulmonary arterial hypertension, causing RV pressure overload.
Why are loop diuretics preferred over thiazides in right‑sided failure? — Loop diuretics act on the thick ascending limb, providing stronger natriuresis needed for significant volume overload.
What feature on echocardiography indicates functional RV impairment despite hypertrophy? — Reduced TAPSE (<16 mm) or RV fractional area change <35 % signals systolic dysfunction.
When is anticoagulation indicated in RVH? — In chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension or documented in‑situ thrombosis to prevent further emboli.
Explain why high‑dose beta‑blockers may be harmful in severe RV pressure overload. — They reduce heart rate and contractility, limiting the RV’s ability to maintain output against high afterload.

A patient from a malaria‑endemic area has RVH – which infection should you specifically screen for and why? — Screen for schistosomiasis, as hepatic involvement can cause portal hypertension and secondary pulmonary hypertension.
ai.title: Right Ventricular Hypertrophy
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH) is the thickening of the right ventricular wall due to chronic pressure or volume overload. It is common in low‑resource settings from pulmonary hypertension, congenital lesions, and chronic lung disease. Recognising RVH guides urgent management and long‑term care.

b: Pressure overload → concentric hypertrophy
Volume overload → eccentric hypertrophy
Common in pulmonary hypertension, COPD, congenital shunts, and chronic thromboembolic disease
sections.p: RVH results when the right ventricle must generate higher pressures or handle larger volumes over time. The myocardium adapts by adding sarcomeres, leading to wall thickening and eventual dysfunction.

b: Echocardiographic RV wall thickness >5 mm (adult) suggests RVH
RV systolic pressure >35 mmHg indicates pulmonary hypertension
RV dilation with reduced TAPSE (<16 mm) signals functional impairment
sections.p: Diagnostic criteria rely on imaging (echocardiography, ECG) and clinical context. Severity is staged by right‑sided pressures and functional class (WHO/NYHA).

b: Symptoms: exertional dyspnoea, peripheral oedema, abdominal fullness
Signs: loud P2, right‑sided S3, hepatomegaly, jugular venous distension
Complications: cor pulmonale, tricuspid regurgitation, thromboembolism
sections.p: RVH predicts morbidity in patients with chronic lung disease, HIV‑related pulmonary hypertension, and rheumatic heart disease. It can progress to right‑sided heart failure, arrhythmias, and sudden death.

t.b: Does the ECG show right‑axis deviation or RV strain? → Right‑axis deviation, R>S in V1, and T‑wave inversion suggest RV overload.
Is there evidence of pulmonary hypertension or lung disease? → Prominent pulmonary arteries, pruning, or enlarged right heart silhouette.
What are RV dimensions, wall thickness, and pressures? → Confirms RVH, estimates pulmonary artery pressure, assesses TAPSE and RV fractional area change.
Is chronic thromboembolic disease present? → Detects obstructive lesions causing pressure overload.

t.a: Serology for HIV, hepatitis B, schistosomiasis
t.b: Are infectious contributors present? → Positive tests guide targeted therapy.

b: Pulmonary hypertension: phosphodiesterase‑5 inhibitors (e.g., sildenafil) if affordable; avoid endothelin antagonists when liver disease is present.
Chronic lung disease: optimise bronchodilators, inhaled steroids, and treat infections promptly.
Rheumatic heart disease: secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin; consider valve surgery when severe.
Right‑sided failure: loop diuretics for congestion, careful fluid balance, and low‑dose aldosterone antagonists if potassium safe.
Avoid high‑dose beta‑blockers that may worsen RV output in severe pressure overload.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then support the right ventricle and monitor for decompensation.

b: LVH shows high voltage QRS in left leads, not right‑axis shift.
Right‑atrial enlargement produces peaked P‑waves (P pulmonale) without RV wall thickening.
sections.p: Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and isolated right‑atrial enlargement can mimic RVH on ECG and imaging.

b: Normal ECG does not exclude RVH if clinical suspicion is high.
Echocardiographic RV wall thickness can be underestimated in poor acoustic windows; use contrast or repeat when possible.
sections.p: In severe obesity or chronic lung disease, ECG voltage criteria may be attenuated, giving a false‑negative RVH.

b: Ask about chronic cough, TB history, HIV status, and exposure to biomass smoke.
Listen for a loud P2 and a right‑sided S3; palpate a parasternal heave.
Use the WHO functional class to grade severity quickly.
sections.p: Focus on functional assessment, bedside signs, and linking the likely cause to the regional disease burden.

b: Prescribing high‑dose ACE inhibitors without assessing RV preload.
Ignoring the need for anticoagulation in chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.
Failing to screen for HIV or schistosomiasis in endemic areas.
sections.p: Misattributing dyspnoea solely to left‑sided disease, overlooking treatable infections, and using left‑sided heart failure drugs that depress RV output.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of dyspnoea with chest pain
Rapidly rising jugular venous pressure with hypotension
